name: Classification — Finding the Number That Doesn't Belong
whatIsIt: Classification (odd-one-out) questions give you a group of numbers where four share a hidden common property and one doesn't. Your job is to figure out the shared rule — not guess which number 'looks different' — and use it to correctly identify the true odd one out.
whyNeeded: This trains you to find the RULE binding a group together, not just spot surface differences. The most common trap is fixating on an obvious-but-wrong property (like 'even vs odd') when the real shared rule is something deeper (like 'perfect squares').
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking, and railway exams
Categorizing and organizing information by shared properties
Data cleaning — spotting the one record that breaks a pattern
Scientific classification and pattern recognition generally

vocabulary.meaning: The one rule that four of the five numbers all follow (e.g. 'is a perfect square', 'is prime').
The single number that does NOT follow the shared property found in the rest.
An obvious but often wrong pattern (like odd/even) that happens to fit by coincidence, not the actual designed rule.

story.title: The Square Numbers Game
story.text: Rohan says: '4, 9, 16, 20, 25 — 20 looks odd because it's the only one not ending in the same pattern.' Divya checks more carefully: 4=2×2, 9=3×3, 16=4×4, 25=5×5 — all perfect squares! But 20 isn't 2×2, 3×3, 4×4, or 5×5 of anything whole. 'It's not about how the number LOOKS,' Divya says, 'it's about whether it fits the actual rule — being a perfect square. 20 is the odd one out because it breaks that rule, not because of a hunch.'
story.answerInStory: 20 — the other four (4, 9, 16, 25) are all perfect squares (2², 3², 4², 5²), but 20 is not.

visual.caption: Test each number against a hidden shared rule — the perfect squares (4, 9, 16, 25) all fit; 20 is the one that breaks the pattern.

teachingGallery.title: Test the majority first, not the guess
teachingGallery.note: Pick any three of the five numbers and find every property they share (square, prime, multiple of something, digit sum). Then check which property the fourth number ALSO fits — that confirms the real rule — before checking the fifth against it.

examples.caption: All look 'small and odd-ish', but the real shared rule here is 'prime number' — 2, 3, 5, 11 are prime, while 9 = 3×3 is not.

standardMethod.summary: List every mathematical property you can think of for three of the five numbers (square, cube, prime, multiple of a number, digit sum, odd/even). Check which property ALL of a group of four numbers share. Confirm the fifth number breaks exactly that property — that is the true odd one out.
steps: Pick any three numbers from the group and list properties they all share (e.g. all prime, all perfect squares, all multiples of 3).
Check a fourth number against each candidate property — keep only the properties that still hold for all four.
Check the fifth number against the surviving property — if it breaks that property, it's confirmed as the odd one out.
Double check by re-verifying the shared property with actual calculations (don't just eyeball it).

alternateMethods.name: Property checklist
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When the pattern isn't obvious at a glance.
steps: Run through a mental checklist for every number: is it prime? a perfect square? a perfect cube? a multiple of 2, 3, 5? does its digit sum follow a pattern?
The property that fits exactly four out of five numbers is the real rule.
alternateMethods.example: 12, 15, 21, 22, 27 — digit sums are 3, 6, 3, 4, 9. Four of these (3,6,3,9) are divisible by 3, but 22's digit sum (4) is not — so 22 is the odd one out.

steps: Check for perfect squares: 4 = 2², 9 = 3², 16 = 4², 25 = 5² — four numbers fit.
Check 20: is it a perfect square of any whole number? 4²=16, 5²=25 — 20 falls between them, not a perfect square.
20 breaks the shared rule (perfect square) that the other four follow.
Check for prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, and 11 each have no divisors other than 1 and themselves — all prime.
Check 9: 9 = 3 × 3, so it has a divisor (3) other than 1 and itself — 9 is NOT prime, it's composite.
9 breaks the shared rule (prime) that the other four follow.

trickPractice.trick: Find the shared rule among four first, not the odd one directly
trickPractice.intro: Never guess the odd one from a hunch — confirm the rule that the OTHER four numbers share, then test the fifth against it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing which number 'looks different' before actually finding and confirming the shared rule of the other four.
commonMistakes.fix: Always identify the property shared by at least four of the numbers FIRST — only then check which one breaks it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Locking onto the first obvious property noticed (like odd/even) instead of checking whether a deeper property (square, prime, multiple) actually fits better.
commonMistakes.fix: If your first guessed property doesn't cleanly separate exactly one number from the rest, try another property — squares, primes, multiples, and digit sums are the most common designed rules.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding an answer without actually calculating (e.g. assuming a number 'looks prime' without checking its factors).
commonMistakes.fix: Always verify with real calculation — factor the number, compute the square root, or add the digits — rather than trusting a first impression.

rememberIt.hook: Find the rule of the four first
rememberIt.unpack: Confirm the shared property among four numbers before naming the fifth as the odd one out.

studentQuestions.q: What if two different properties both seem to almost work?
studentQuestions.a: Check both against ALL five numbers carefully — a properly designed question has exactly one property that fits four numbers perfectly and fails for exactly one; if two properties both seem to fit, you likely haven't checked all five numbers against each one yet.

studentQuestions.q: Are there other properties besides squares, primes, and multiples?
studentQuestions.a: Yes — digit sums, cubes, numbers one more/less than a square, or even patterns like 'each number is double the previous' can all be the hidden rule. Keep a mental checklist and test methodically.
